Look at bark and leaf texture together: Chinese elm has distinctive exfoliating mottled tan/orange/gray bark and small glossy, mostly singly serrate leaves; it flowers and fruits in late summer-fall.
Familiar aromatic-hairy scrambling plant with compound/divided leaves, yellow flowers, and large fleshy berries that ripen red, yellow, orange, or other cultivated colors.

LOOK HERE FIRST: find stiff, sharply angled green stems that appear almost leafless; inspect the nodes for clusters of tiny separate male or female flowers. Confirm minute alternate scale-like upper leaves and reddish fringed stipules rather than assuming the green shoots are gra

LOOK HERE FIRST: Opposite SIMPLE leaves with one blade deeply palmately divided into usually 5–7 pointed, finely toothed lobes; verify opposite buds and paired winged samaras. Cultivars vary widely in leaf shape and color; red foliage alone is not diagnostic.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Check for a persistent woody shrub with many short gray-green wedge-shaped leaves, commonly ending in three short rounded teeth. Confirm gray-brown woody stems and, when present, upright sprays of tiny heads. Three tips alone are not proof: compare the shrub habi
Treat as a nursery/lookalike comparison: pinnate evergreen leaves with many holly-like leaflets and blue-purple berry clusters. It is not native to Texas under the current Kew concept.

Start at a middle or upper leaf node: the opposite narrow leaves have rounded ear-like (auriculate), often clasping bases. Follow the leaf axil to a loose, stalked cyme with several tiny flowers; inspect the ribbed floral tube, then a mature globose capsule. Compare cluster stalk

LOOK HERE FIRST: Single fan-shaped leaves with repeatedly FORKING (dichotomous) veins, often notched at tip; leaves cluster on short spur shoots. Female trees bear fleshy-coated naked seeds, not berries or drupes.

Inspect the tiny bract halfway along each flower stalk (pedicel), then the short raceme peduncle and flower center. Five sterile stamens (staminodes) help separate this species from bractless Samolus ebracteatus. A leaf rosette alone cannot settle the identification.

Compare the collar/ligule and mature awned spikelets with S. nutans, then check the whole plant. S. elliottii is the slender eastern sandy-woodland Indiangrass comparison; S. nutans is generally more robust with a conspicuous ligule and dense golden panicle. Habitat alone cannot
Provisional learner for the old Thelesperma ambiguum concept; use alongside other greenthreads until project taxonomy/range is tightened.
Look for hairiness before the airy panicle: conspicuously hirsute leaf sheaths plus distinctly bearded panicle branch axils are the strongest combination.

Texas groundplum variety with thick green fleshy pods near the ground. The important look-alike is A. plattensis: compare ovary/pod HAIRS (groundplum generally glabrous versus hairy plattensis) and groove along each pod SUTURE, not just the pod's size.
Woody shrub or small tree with stiff branchlets, small leaves and dark drupes; examine branching, armature and fruits against related Condalia and Ziziphus.

Look for the flower architecture: five red petals remain tightly furled rather than spreading flat, while the staminal column and style project conspicuously beyond them. Then confirm the stellate-hairy, cordate to shallowly 3-lobed leaves.
Bushy submerged watermilfoil with feather-like whorled leaves and emergent flowering shoots that transition to broader serrate bracts.

FIRST inspect a mid-stem leaf's two surfaces and edge: S. lanceolatum generally has pliable, nonwaxy, comparatively flat leaves with diffuse or elongated lower-surface vein AREOLES, unlike S. praealtum with firmer waxy upper faces and conspicuous small isodiametric lower areoles.
Look for the mostly unlobed to shallowly toothed, leathery evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves. The acorn cup is deeper than in Shumard oak and may enclose roughly half the nut.

more_review_candidates.review_prompt: Think tall, glaucous perennial with highly dissected fingerlike leaves and NO involucellar bractlets. The inflorescence is paniculate, stipules are usually shed early, and the calyx lobes meet into a pointed bud.
Look for a cool-season, wispy bunchgrass with a loose panicle and single extremely long twisted awns. Each fertile floret carries one awn—not the three-awned fork of Aristida.

Start with the tiny wiry reddish plant and narrow appressed seedhead branches. Red grama is a short perennial bunchgrass with very narrow mostly basal leaves and 2–7 small persistent red to purplish pectinate branches held close to the main axis.

Start with scale and the ligule. Lindheimer muhly is a large dense fountain-form bunchgrass, commonly around 1 m or more tall, with unusually long conspicuous membranous ligules and a tall feathery panicle. It dwarfs seep muhly and is completely unlike creeping nimblewill.
Feel or closely inspect the broad leaves: this is the big sandpaper-textured Verbena, with broad ovate leaves and long, thin flowering spikes that can form a branched panicle.

Start with the leaves and flower spikes. Hall's prairie clover is a slender perennial with mostly 3-foliolate leaves, sparse wiry stems, and relatively loose spikes of conspicuous yellow flowers. The calyx ribs/teeth are often reddish-brown and hairy.
Long hairs at the sheath throat/collar + glabrous culm nodes + a huge diffuse fine-branched panicle on a tall perennial bunchgrass.
Start with habit and leaflet size: a xeric shrub or small tree with tiny leathery, often nearly evergreen leaflets—commonly only three per leaf.

Think glossy narrow red-oak-type foliage: Canby oak has dark glossy evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves with serrated to bristle-tipped margins and a distinctly horticultural landscape presence in Texas.

needs_more_source_photos.review_prompt: Start with the woody shrub habit and long red-orange tubular flowers. Flame acanthus is a many-stemmed deciduous shrub with opposite narrow leaves and terminal clusters of narrow two-lipped hummingbird flowers.
Low annual with axillary flower clusters from base to top; the cluster axes become thick, inflated and hard at maturity, with uniquely keeled flower bracts.
Start with the compound leaf: many narrow lance-shaped leaflets sit along a conspicuously winged rachis. Then confirm the deciduous, clonal shrub/small-tree habit and vivid red fall color.

Look for a low, densely hairy plant with dark maroon-to-brown star-shaped flowers, commonly paired close to the stem and heart-shaped leaves. Then inspect the milkweed gynostegium in the flower center.
Look for a vigorous twining vine with large opposite cordate leaves, relatively large uniform olive-green star-shaped flowers, and a long smooth follicle with strong longitudinal angles.

Like Texas snakeweed, an open and wispy yellow-flowering annual. Examine the back of a real flower head: pale/resinous phyllaries without green midnerve borders; then the DISC floret has long white basally united pappus scales, unlike G. texana's nearly absent/very short scales.

Start with life cycle, foliage, and ray pattern. Rock tickseed is an annual with narrow linear leaves and slender branching stems; the yellow ray florets usually carry rusty-red/brown color at the base.

Start with the lower leaves: in local var. texanum, broad serrate blades narrow into winged petioles, while tiny narrow leaves occur high on the flowering branches. Distal stems are densely hairy and widely spreading branches have densely short-bracted flower stalks. FNA var. tex

LOOK AT A REAL LEAF CLOSE-UP FIRST: both leaf faces and outer phyllaries are densely coated in separate, long, SILVERY, SOFT HAIRS lying near-parallel to the surface (sericeous hairs). At hand-lens scale, follow individual white hairs across the green blade; a silvery glare alone
Expect an intermediate ironweed. Plants occur where western ironweed and woolly ironweed meet, with foliage, hairiness, leaf width, and head characters falling between the parents.
Yellow-flowered bladderpod whose upper leaves are notably sessile, helping separate it from more obviously petiolate relatives.

Find an areole before anything else. On the flattened green cladodes, each areole is a specialized short shoot that can carry hairs, glochids, permanent spines, flowers, or new pads. Then compare pad shape, spine/glochid pattern, yellow-to-orange flower, and beet-red berry.

Compare the whole plant against Texas pricklypear before counting spines. O. macrorhiza is usually a low, sprawling grassland cactus with smaller pads close to the ground. Then check the areoles: relatively few permanent spines, often with the main spine strongly bent or deflexed

Start with the narrow leaves and the stem hairs. Prairie spiderwort has narrow linear to strap-shaped leaves and conspicuous long-stalked glandular hairs on the internodes and peduncles. In the Williamson treatment the blades are about 6–17 mm wide, giving the plant a noticeably
Low gray prairie subshrub with densely silky compound leaves and narrow upright violet-purple flower spikes.
Texas annual milkvetch in the Nuttallianus complex with 4–12 flowers per raceme, relatively broad leaflets, and long narrow glabrous pods.
Compare leaf breadth, lower-surface pubescence, acorn shape, geography, and Q. fusiformis overlap. Ambiguous Central Texas live oaks should remain unresolved.

First look at the plant base and leaf tips. Wright's skullcap is a low bushy perennial with many stems from a persistent base and small entire leaves with rounded/obtuse tips. Its hairs are minute and the calyx can look nearly smooth to the naked eye. Then confirm the larger upwa

Start with the fluffy head. Bushy bluestem makes dense broomlike to cottony clusters near the top of the plant, with paired short rames packed inside and emerging from upper leaf sheaths. The inflorescence looks bushy rather than like separate turkey-foot fingers.

Start with one mature intact spikelet: LOWER and UPPER glumes are normally similar in length (about 18–25 mm without their terminal awns); the lower glume often shows THREE TO SEVEN veins when backlit. Then check that the plant is a wiry, freely branched ANNUAL without a persiste

Check the stem nodes before the seedhead. Cane bluestem has a conspicuous dense beard/ring of soft hairs around the node, often several millimeters long. Then confirm the fanlike silvery panicle: many primary branches spread nearly as long as the main inflorescence.

Start with the seedhead and nodes. King Ranch bluestem has smooth/glabrous nodes and a loose terminal head of only about 3–8 long fingerlike branches. The stems often kink/change angle at nodes and branch freely from a broad crown. That is very different from silver bluestem's de
Annual habit + coarse many-flowered spikelets + crater-like glands on panicle branches, pedicels, glumes or lemma keels.

Start at the panicle and sheath collar. Plains lovegrass is a tufted perennial with an extremely open, airy panicle whose tiny spikelets sit on long divergent pedicels. Leaf sheaths are mostly glabrous, with hairs concentrated near the sheath apex/collar rather than being shaggy
Look for a tufted perennial lovegrass with very narrow, firm, inward-rolled leaves and a comparatively restrained panicle rather than the broad airy cloud of purple lovegrass.
Look for dense clusters of spikelets packed along the panicle branches. The spikelets often become violet to reddish, giving the inflorescence a heavier, chunkier look than purple lovegrass.
Ignore the old Panicum label and look at the runners: long wiry stolons with swollen woolly nodes root to make new plants, while narrow upright seedheads rise from the sod.

Forget the ornamental-muhly silhouette: nimblewill is low and weak. Look for decumbent much-branched stems that root at the lower nodes, short flat blades, and a narrow contracted panicle. That creeping/rooting habit separates it instantly from the two upright bunchgrasses.

Think intermediate between Lindheimer muhly and seep muhly: a dense upright perennial bunchgrass with firm folded leaves and an open erect panicle, usually in rocky canyons and prairie openings where the parent ranges overlap.
Look for hair plus chaos: witchgrass is an annual with conspicuously hairy sheaths/nodes and an enormous, extremely open many-branched panicle that can look like a tumbleweed.
Small Texas fluffgrass relative with a compact seedhead and conspicuous cottony or fluffy hairs around the spikelets at maturity.

Look at the flowering spike before anything else: a thick corn-relative spike has male spikelets on the upper portion and hard bead-like female spikelets below, all rising from a huge broad-leaved rhizomatous clump.

Look for the gray cast before anything else: this is the short, low vervain whose stems and leaves are densely covered in stiff whitish hairs, giving the entire plant a canescent or dusty-gray appearance.
